query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a reactive surface modification that promotes the in situ formation of a high-temperature–stable, lubricious oxide layer on the CoCrFeNi alloy surface will maintain a low coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix with conventional microstructure and sliding tribological response that degrades at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: A single-stage reactive surface treatment (e.g., via controlled deposition or surface doping) that induces the formation of a thin, continuous lubricious oxide (likely enriched in chromium and/or other alloying elements) during sliding.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests conducted under a constant load and in controlled ambient atmosphere, spanning a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultrathin, high-temperature–stable lubricious oxide layer at the tribological interface that serves as a protective, low-shear film.
generation.mechanism: The reactive treatment enables the alloy surface to rapidly form a self-adaptive oxide tribolayer during sliding. At lower temperatures, the layer reduces direct metal–metal contact to lower friction and wear, while at higher temperatures, it prevents deleterious oxidation and excessive wear by providing a thermally robust, lubricious interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated CoCrFeNi, the treated alloy will exhibit consistently lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range, with performance at elevated temperatures approaching or exceeding that observed in other self-lubricating systems.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the tribological performance (higher friction and wear rate at high temperature, with friction coefficient deteriorating notably above room temperature) of the as-processed CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid under sliding conditions with similar loads and environmental atmospheres as those in earlier studies, specifically from room temperature up to 800 °C. It does not address behavior under significantly different loading or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact chemical composition and thickness of the oxide layer required, its long-term stability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads, and potential interactions with varying environments beyond controlled laboratory conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set subjected to the reactive surface modification (intervention) and one untreated control. Conduct sliding wear tests under identical loads and ambient conditions at temperatures of RT, 300 °C, 500 °C, and 800 °C. Evaluate the formation, continuity, and stability of the oxide layer via surface characterization (e.g., XPS, SEM) after testing.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate (material loss) measured at each temperature
Surface chemical and microstructural analysis of the tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reactive surface treatment does not lead to a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the temperature range compared to the untreated baseline, or if the lubricious oxide layer is not observed to form or remain stable during sliding, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
